In brief

Parody. "The catastrophe was terrific and instantaneous in its effect [...] K. G., K. P., K. T., P. C., K. C. B., M. P, J. P., M. B., D. S. O., S. O. D., M. F. H., M. R. I. A., B. L., Mus. Doc., P. L. G., F. T. C. D., F. R. U. I., F. R. C. P. I. and F. R. C. S. I": the Citizen's attack on Bloom in his preferred manner—hurling metal objects—is presented hyperbolically as a devastating earthquake and a "cyclonic" windstorm. The conjunction of the two phenomena is explained by a suggestion that a large meteor has streaked through the atmosphere and rocked the planet. The newspaper-like reportage of the previous parody continues here, this time with less society-page gushing and more scientific terminology.

At more length

The cyclopean hyperbole begins even before the parody does, when the narrator expresses awe at the Citizen's arm strength: "Mercy of God the sun was in his eyes or he'd have left him for dead. Gob, he near sent it into the county Longford." Never mind that the weapon is an empty tin box that has little chance of making it into the next street, much less the County Longford far to the northwest (it goes "clattering along the street"). Never mind that a projectile of such light weight and high wind resistance could hardly be thrown accurately or do worse than raise a welt. As a former shotput champion the Citizen's ability to launch an iron ball some fifteen or twenty meters means that he should be able to send a lighter object almost to the moon, with laser-like targeting.

The parody, adopting the style of a newspaper reporting on a natural "catastrophe," details the effects of the object's launch and its landing. As measured by "The observatory of Dunsink," there were eleven seismic "shocks, all of the fifth grade of Mercalli's scale." Giuseppe Mercalli (1850-1914) was an Italian seismologist who invented a scale for assessing the magnitude of an earthquake's effects on surface structures. Given the context, one would expect "the fifth grade" to be the highest, and Gifford judges that the Citizen's earthquake would be "as heavy as any that had ever been recorded on a seismograph to that date." Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner, however, report that Mercalli's scale had twelve levels, meaning that these shocks "would cause only moderate damage." The disagreement stems from the fact that Mercalli's scale was amended several times. As first formulated in 1883 it had six levels. A second scale, published in 1902, had ten. In 1904 Adolfo Cancani proposed adding two new categories denominated "Catastrophe" and "Enormous Catastrophe," for a total of twelve. A slightly modified form of that one is still in use today. It is hard to say which version Joyce knew of or how well he understood it, but it seems safe to assume that he had a very great magnitude in mind.

Continuing its scientific language, the parody locates the "epicentre" in the general vicinity of Barney Kiernan's and observes that the "seismic waves" destroyed many buildings in the area. Strangely, witnesses have sworn that the shocks were "accompanied by a violent atmospheric perturbation of cyclonic character." The newspaper article substantiates this claim of winds rotating with great force by noting that "search parties" found the hat of a court clerk on "the third basaltic ridge of the giant's causeway," in the far northeast of Ireland, and a judge's umbrella "embedded to the extent of one foot three inches in the sandy beach of Holeopen bay near the old head of Kinsale," on the southwestern coast. As in the previous parody, where celebratory fires were lit on mountains and coastlines all over Ireland, these cyclonic winds have covered the entire island, sending things flying in every direction.

Major earthquakes do not typically coincide with major hurricanes or typhoons. Clearly the implication is that, before the Citizen's biscuit tin landed with an earthshaking thud, its immense velocity somehow imparted violent circular motion to the air. The parody relates the two forces by means of a third: "Other eyewitnesses depose that they observed an incandescent object of enormous proportions hurtling through the atmosphere at a terrifying velocity in a trajectory directed southwest by west." This original natural phenomenon, an immense meteor plunging through the atmosphere, has caused the other two.

The pseudo-science is complicated enough, but the parody also plays off the Citizen's militant nationalism by incorporating several indications of disrespect for Ireland's ruling authorities. It notes that there is "no record extant of a similar seismic disturbance in our island since the earthquake of 1534, the year of the rebellion of Silken Thomas." In that year of a great earthquake, recorded in the 1904 Thom's Dublin Annals (2093), the son of the Earl of Kildare set off a political earthquake by proclaiming himself a rebel to the English crown and attacking Dublin Castle. The earthquake of 1904 also has a political impact, destroying "All the lordly residences in the vicinity of the palace of justice" as well as the courthouse itself, "in which at the time of the catastrophe important legal debates were in progress," leaving "a mass of ruins beneath which it is to be feared all the occupants have been buried alive." Officers of the court lose not only their headgear and umbrellas but also their lives.

A final subversive gesture appears at the end of the parody. The work of picking through the ruins falls to two local contractors and to some British troops led by a fictional rear admiral. His name, "sir Hercules Hannibal Habeas Corpus Anderson," is impossibly inflated, and so are the abbreviated titles representing his many accomplishments: Knight of the Garter, Knight of the Order of Saint Patrick, Knight of the Thistle, Privy Councilor, Knight Commander of the Bath, Member of Parliament, Justice of the Peace, Bachelor of Medicine, Distinguished Service Order, Sodomite, Master of Fox Hounds, Member of the Royal Irish Academy, Bachelor of Laws or of Letters, Doctor of Music, Poor Law Guardian, Fellow of Trinity College Dublin, Fellow of the Royal University of Ireland, Fellow of the Royal College of Physicians of Ireland, Fellow of the Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland.

The previous parody allowed one detail, a place name containing a crude intestinal joke, to deflate all the overblown praises of Bloom as a visiting monarch. This one does the same thing. Although no human being could hope to attain all the honors heaped on Sir Hercules, the honors themselves are real, except for one wee whimsical moment when DSO becomes SOD. This stands for nothing but Bugger.

John Hunt 2026
